◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
In the funnel example, why is public money or an offtake commitment 
most valuable at the last gate?
A The last gate is the cheapest stage
B It holds about 78% of the spend while commercial returns are still unproven
C Research grants already cover it fully
D Banks always lend freely at that stage
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. It holds about 78% of the spend while 
commercial returns are still unproven
Stage C costs ₹4,000 crore of the ₹5,100 crore total, 
yet revenue is not proven until plants operate. 
Guaranteed demand and public capital reduce that 
risk enough for private money to follow.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 20

S E C T I O N 3 O F 4
Sustainable Business Models
A technology only matters if someone can profitably deliver it to many people.
21

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E F R A M E W O R K
Bocken’s Eight Sustainable Business Model Archetypes
Grouped by Bocken, Short, Rana and Evans (2014) into technological, social, and organisational innovation.
Maximise Efficiency
Technological: do more with less material and 
energy, through lightweighting and lean 
design.
Value from “Waste”
Technological: treat one process’s residue as 
another’s input, as in industrial symbiosis.
Substitute with Renewables
Technological: replace fossil inputs with 
renewable energy and natural processes.
Functionality, Not Ownership
Social: sell the service or outcome and keep 
the asset, as in leasing and pay-per-use.
Stewardship
Social: take responsibility for the long-run 
welfare of stakeholders and resources.
Sufficiency
Social: encourage lower consumption 
through durability, repair, and moderation.
Re-purpose for Society
Organisational: put social or environmental 
mission at the core of the company.
Scale-up Solutions
Organisational: replicate impact quickly 
through partnerships, franchising, and open 
designs.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 22

S E C T I O N 3 · I N P R A C T I C E
Each Archetype Has Real-World Examples
Illustrations of how the archetypes show up in different industries.
Maximise Efficiency Lightweight packaging, lean manufacturing, and energy-efficient product design.
Value from “Waste” Industrial symbiosis, such as Kalundborg in Denmark, where firms exchange steam, water, and by-products.
Substitute with Renewables Solar PV replacing diesel generators; bio-based materials replacing fossil-based ones.
Functionality, Not Ownership Lighting-as-a-service, mobility subscriptions, and battery leasing.
Stewardship Certified supply chains such as Fairtrade and FSC; take-back and responsible sourcing.
Sufficiency Durable, repairable products and repair services, such as Patagonia’s Worn Wear programme.
Re-purpose for Society Social enterprises, including pay-as-you-go solar for off-grid households.
Scale-up Solutions Open-source designs, franchising, and partnerships that let others replicate quickly.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 23

S E C T I O N 3 · A D E S I G N T O O L
The Layered Business Model Canvas
The Business Model Canvas (Osterwalder and Pigneur) describes how a company creates and captures value. Joyce and Paquin (2016) extended it to three 
layers.
Economic Layer The familiar canvas: value proposition, customers, channels, revenue streams, cost structure, key partners, 
resources, and activities.
Environmental Layer A life-cycle view of the same model (materials, production, distribution, use, end-of-life) showing environmental 
impacts and benefits. In effect, LCA on the canvas.
Social Layer A stakeholder view: who is affected, and what social impacts and benefits (jobs, access, health, community) the 
model creates or removes.
Why Use It It puts value, hidden costs, and affected people on one page, so a team can test whether profit relies on impacts 
someone else pays for.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 24

S E C T I O N 3 · A K E Y A R C H E T Y P E
Selling a Product vs. Selling an Outcome
Selling a Product Product-as-a-Service
Revenue arrives once, at the sale. Profit rises with units sold. Revenue arrives over time, per use or per period. Profit rises with uptime and 
long life.
The seller has little reason to design for long life or easy repair; durability can 
reduce future sales.
The seller keeps ownership, so durable, repairable, upgradeable design lowers 
its own costs.
The customer carries performance, maintenance, and end-of-life risk. The provider carries those risks and needs data to manage them: a natural role 
for IoT and software.
Barriers are modest: familiar to customers, finance teams, and accountants. Barriers: capital tied up in assets, customer trust, new contracts, and pricing 
for use.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 25

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
When a Systems Innovation Fails to Scale: Better Place
Better Place (2007–2013): swappable batteries as a service
Better Place sold electric cars without batteries: drivers leased the battery and swapped it for a fresh one at automated stations in minutes. It raised about US$850 
million from investors including HSBC, Morgan Stanley, and GE, and went into liquidation in 2013.
The Idea
Separate car from battery to cut upfront cost and remove range anxiety. It was product-as￾a-service logic applied to the most expensive component.
The Numbers
Well under 2,000 cars were deployed across Israel and Denmark by most accounts, and 
only a few dozen swap stations were built, against an early forecast of 100,000 cars on 
Israeli roads by 2010.
Why It Failed
Heavy infrastructure spending before revenue; one car model from one manufacturing 
partner; leasing firms and drivers unconvinced of the economics; permit and rollout delays.
The Lesson
A sound idea can fail on ecosystem coordination, capital intensity, and timing. Swapping is 
now being retried mainly for fleets and small vehicles, where standard batteries and 
predictable routes help.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 26

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
A provider installs lighting, keeps ownership, and charges customers 
per unit of light delivered. Which archetype is this?
A Encourage sufficiency
B Create value from waste
C Deliver functionality, rather than ownership
D Develop scale-up solutions
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. Deliver functionality, rather than 
ownership
Selling an outcome while retaining the asset is the 
“functionality rather than ownership” archetype. It 
aligns the provider’s profit with durable, efficient, 
repairable design.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 28

S E C T I O N 4 O F 4
Innovating Responsibly
The best innovation solves the problem without moving it somewhere else.
29

S E C T I O N 4 · U N I N T E N D E D C O N S E Q U E N C E S
Rebound, Problem-Shifting, and Responsible Innovation
Innovation can backfire in predictable ways, which means it can be managed.
Rebound Effects Efficiency gains can be partly or fully offset by extra use (the Jevons paradox from our principles lecture), so 
innovation needs caps or price signals beside it.
Problem-Shifting Solving one problem can create another: battery minerals and their supply chains, panel and battery end-of-life, 
and the electricity demand of data centres. An LCA lens catches these early.
Four Habits of Responsible Innovation Stilgoe, Owen and Macnaghten (2013): anticipate impacts, reflect on assumptions, include affected people, and 
respond by changing course.
Who Gets the Benefit? Technologies priced for rich markets may not reach communities most exposed to climate impacts. Social equity 
applies to innovation too.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 30

S E C T I O N 4 · F O R E C A S T I N G H U M I L I T Y
Even the IEA’s Technology Forecasts Moved
Between the 2021 and 2023 editions of its net-zero roadmap, some technologies surged and others stalled.
What Slipped Solid-state battery prototypes saw production delays; fuel-cell electric vehicles have not reached the market 
potential once foreseen; carbon capture on power plants is moving more slowly than projected.
What Surged Key clean technologies saw record growth, and the share of 2050 reductions from not-yet-marketed 
technologies fell from almost half to around 35%.
The Planning Lesson Think in portfolios: back many options, expect most to miss (our funnel example: 14 of 100 survive), and be 
ready to scale winners fast.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 31

S E C T I O N 4 · Y O U R O W N F I E L D
Green Software: The Software Carbon Intensity (SCI) 
Standard
For computer scientists, innovation for sustainability includes making software itself lower-carbon.
What It Is ISO/IEC 21031:2024, published March 2024, from the Green Software Foundation: a method to calculate the 
carbon emission rate of a software system.
The Formula SCI = ((E × I) + M) per R. E = energy used (kWh); I = carbon intensity of the grid where and when it runs 
(gCO₂e/kWh); M = embodied hardware emissions; R = functional unit (per user, request, or transaction).
Why “Per R” Matters R is the LCA functional unit again. A rate lets you compare designs and track progress as usage grows: totals can 
rise while the rate falls.
What It Excludes Offsets and credits cannot lower an SCI score. Only real reductions in E, I, or M count, consistent with our view 
of offset quality.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 32

S E C T I O N 4 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Calculating and Lowering a Software Carbon Intensity Score
G I V E N
An API handles R = 1,000 requests using E = 0.5 kWh of server energy
Grid carbon intensity where it runs: I = 700 gCO₂e/kWh
Embodied hardware emissions attributed to this workload: M = 20 gCO₂e 
(illustrative)
F O R M U L A
SCI = ((E × I) + M) per R
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Operational part: 0.5 kWh × 700 gCO₂e/kWh = 350 gCO₂e
2 SCI = 350 + 20 = 370 gCO₂e per 1,000 requests
3 Option 1, move to a cleaner region (I = 100): (0.5 × 100) + 20 = 70, a fall of 81%
4 Option 2, halve the energy by optimising code (E = 0.25): (0.25 × 700) + 20 = 195, a fall of 47%
370 → 70 or 195 Both options beat buying offsets, which cannot lower SCI. Which is better depends on grid mix and effort; the best designs do both. 
(All figures are illustrative.)
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 33

“Pick one: green hydrogen, battery swapping, or AI￾designed materials. Where does it sit on the readiness

what could go wrong?”

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
In SCI = ((E × I) + M) per R, which action can NOT lower the score?
A Running the workload where the grid is cleaner
B Optimising code so it uses less energy
C Purchasing carbon offsets
D Extending the life of the hardware that runs the workload
A N S W E R & W H Y
C. Purchasing carbon offsets
SCI counts real emissions: energy (E), grid carbon 
intensity (I), and embodied hardware emissions (M). 
Offsets and credits are explicitly not a way to reduce 
an SCI score.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 35

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
Five Questions for Any Sustainable Innovation
Use these before backing, building, or buying a new technology or business model.
1. Does It Hit a Hotspot? Does it address a material impact found by LCA or Scope 3 analysis, rather than only an easy one?
2. Where Is It on the Ladder? What is its TRL, and who funds the next gate (grant, blended finance, offtake)?
3. What Model Gets It Adopted? Which archetype aligns the provider’s profit with durability and customer value?
4. What Could Go Wrong? Rebound, problem-shifting, supply-chain risk, end-of-life, and who is left out.
5. Can We Prove It? Is there an evidence file (LCA, EPD, SCI score) that survives CCPA- and EU-style claim rules?
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 36

B R I N G I N G I T T O G E T H E R
Innovation Connects Every Business Function
The functions covered in this series each supply something innovation needs.
R&D / Design Runs the TRL pipeline and builds LCA into every stage gate.
Finance Bridges the valley of death with grants, blended finance, and green bonds for first-of-a-kind assets.
Procurement Secures critical materials responsibly and tests supplier innovations.
Operations Hosts pilots and scales what works.
Marketing Tests real demand and communicates claims credibly.
Legal & IT Protect IP, manage regulation, and build the data pipelines (SCI, LCA) that prove impact.
INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 37

“You lead innovation at a mid-size Indian manufacturer. 
Pick one product or process and pitch in three minutes:

INNOVATION & SUSTAINABILITY 38

Measuring & Reporting
Sustainability Performance
Key metrics, frameworks, and reporting standards
01

B E F O R E W E B E G I N
The rulebook for sustainability reporting is being rewritten 
as we speak.
The discipline underneath it is not.
ISSB standards adopted by 28 jurisdictions, the EU cutting mandatory datapoints by about 60%, India’s assurance net 
widening to the top 1,000 companies, and new GRI climate rules from 2027. Whatever the framework: define the metric, 
set the boundary, prove the number.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 02

T O D A Y ’ S J O U R N E Y
From a Number to a Credible Disclosure
Earlier lectures taught you to calculate footprints and read BRSR and ISSB at a glance. Today covers the full chain: which metrics to track, which framework to report 
under, how the data becomes a disclosure, and how it earns trust.
01
Choosing the Right 
Metrics
What makes a good metric, absolute 
versus intensity, and targets that follow 
the science.
02
The Framework 
Landscape
GRI, ISSB, TCFD, CDP, GHG Protocol, 
SBTi, ESRS and BRSR, and how they 
converge.
03
From Data to Disclosure
Materiality, boundaries, base years, data 
quality, and the ESG data pipeline.
04
Credibility & Assurance
Limited and reasonable assurance, ISSA 
5000, warning signs, and the road ahead.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 04

S E C T I O N 1 O F 4
Choosing the Right Metrics
Everything downstream (frameworks, assurance, targets) depends on measuring the right thing.
05

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E S T A N D A R D F O R A M E T R I C
Five Tests of a Good Sustainability Metric
Run any proposed indicator through these before adding it to a dashboard or a report.
Relevant
Tied to a material impact or 
risk of this business, not a 
metric that is merely easy to 
collect.
Measurable
Defined with a unit, formula, 
and data source so two people 
get the same number.
Comparable
Consistent over time and 
across peers: same boundary, 
same method, same units.
Verifiable
Backed by evidence an 
independent party can test: 
meters, invoices, contracts.
Actionable
Moves when someone acts. A 
metric nobody can influence is 
reporting, not management.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 06

S E C T I O N 1 · T Y P E S O F M E T R I C
Inputs, Outputs, Outcomes, and Leading vs. Lagging
A balanced scorecard mixes types, because each answers a different question.
Inputs Resources and effort committed: renewable electricity purchased, training hours, R&D spend.
Outputs Direct results of activity: kWh saved, tonnes of waste diverted, suppliers audited.
Outcomes Real-world change: emissions avoided, injury rates falling, water stress reduced. The hardest to measure and the 
most meaningful.
Leading vs. Lagging Leading indicators predict (near-misses reported, supplier audits completed); lagging indicators record what 
happened (lost-time injuries, annual emissions). Good dashboards pair both.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 07

S E C T I O N 1 · T H E C O R E F A M I L I E S
Five Families of Sustainability Metrics
Most frameworks draw from these families, which is why one dataset can serve many reports.
Climate & Energy Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions (tCO₂e); energy consumed (GJ or MWh) and renewable share; emissions intensity.
Water & Waste Water withdrawal and consumption (m³), including in water-stressed areas; waste generated and diversion rate.
Nature Land use, sites near sensitive areas, and the share of deforestation-free sourcing.
People Lost-time injury frequency rate (injuries × 1,000,000 ÷ hours worked); gender diversity; training; fair wages.
Governance Board independence, ethics and anti-corruption training, supplier code compliance, data-privacy incidents.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 08

S E C T I O N 1 · A C R I T I C A L C H O I C E
Absolute vs. Intensity Metrics
Absolute Metric Intensity Metric
Total emissions in tCO₂e, regardless of how much the company produces. Emissions per unit of activity: per ₹ crore revenue, per tonne of product, per 
employee.
Answers: is our contribution to atmospheric carbon actually falling? Answers: are we getting more efficient per unit of output?
Used by science-based targets and carbon-budget logic. Used for benchmarking, for growing firms, and in India’s intensity-based CCTS 
targets.
Risk: can look like failure for a company that grows while cutting waste. Risk: can show progress while the total keeps rising (see next slide).
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 09

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
When Intensity Falls but Total Emissions Rise
G I V E N
Year 1: 100,000 tCO₂e emitted on revenue of ₹1,000 crore
Year 5: revenue grows 30% to ₹1,300 crore
Year 5: emissions intensity (tCO₂e per ₹ crore) is 20% lower than Year 1
F O R M U L A
Absolute Emissions = Intensity × Activity
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Year 1 intensity: 100,000 ÷ 1,000 = 100 tCO₂e per ₹ crore
2 Year 5 intensity: 100 × (1 − 0.20) = 80 tCO₂e per ₹ crore
3 Year 5 absolute: 80 × 1,300 = 104,000 tCO₂e
4 Change in absolute emissions: (104,000 − 100,000) ÷ 100,000 = +4%
+4% Absolute A 20% intensity improvement coincided with higher total emissions. Honest reports show both numbers, because they answer 
different questions. (Figures are illustrative.)
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 10

S E C T I O N 1 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
A Science-Based Glide Path: The 4.2% Rule
G I V E N
Base year 2020 Scope 1+2 emissions: 100,000 tCO₂e
SBTi minimum for a 1.5°C-aligned target: 4.2% of base-year emissions per year, 
linear
Target year 2030 (ten years after the base year)
F O R M U L A
Target Emissions = Base − (4.2% × Base × Years)
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Annual reduction: 0.042 × 100,000 = 4,200 tCO₂e per year
2 Ten-year reduction: 4,200 × 10 = 42,000 tCO₂e (42%)
3 2030 target: 100,000 − 42,000 = 58,000 tCO₂e
4 Mid-point check: the 2025 path value is 79,000; actual 85,000 would be 6,000 tCO₂e off track
58,000 t by 2030 The SBTi’s minimum near-term ambition for Scope 1+2 is a 42% cut by 2030 from a 2020 base. Its April 2026 update adjusts annual 
rates for later base years while keeping the 4.2% floor.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 11

◆ INTERACTIVE C H E C K Y O U R U N D E R S T A N D I N G
A company cuts emissions intensity by 20% while revenue grows 30%. 
What happens to its absolute emissions?
A They fall by about 20%
B They rise by about 4%
C They stay exactly the same
D They rise by 30%
A N S W E R & W H Y
B. They rise by about 4%
Absolute = intensity × activity, so 0.80 × 1.30 = 1.04. 
Intensity targets can hide rising totals, which is why 
science-based targets use absolute reductions.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 12

S E C T I O N 2 O F 4
The Framework Landscape
Many frameworks, different audiences, and a slow convergence toward one global baseline.
13

S E C T I O N 2 · T H E L A N D S C A P E
Six Names You Will Meet
They are not interchangeable: some set what to disclose, some how to count, some how ambitious to be.
GRI
Global Reporting Initiative: impact-focused standards covering 
an organisation’s effects on the economy, environment, and 
people. Voluntary, with universal standards since 2023.
ISSB (IFRS S1 & S2)
Investor-focused baseline for sustainability and climate 
disclosure, built on TCFD and SASB. Applies only where a 
jurisdiction adopts it.
TCFD
A four-pillar climate disclosure structure (governance, strategy, 
risk management, metrics and targets). Disbanded in 2023; 
monitoring passed to the IFRS Foundation.
CDP
A disclosure platform where companies answer standard 
climate, water and forest questionnaires requested by investors 
and buyers.
GHG Protocol & SBTi
The accounting rules for emissions (Scopes 1, 2, 3) and the 
initiative that validates science-based targets.
ESRS & BRSR
Regulatory formats: the EU’s ESRS under CSRD, and SEBI’s BRSR 
for India’s top 1,000 listed companies.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 14

S E C T I O N 2 · M A T E R I A L I T Y
Three Materiality Lenses
The single biggest difference between frameworks is which question they ask about each topic.
Impact Materiality (GRI) How does the organisation affect the economy, environment, and people, whether or not it affects profit? Audience: all 
stakeholders.
Financial Materiality (ISSB) Which sustainability-related risks and opportunities could affect the company’s prospects and enterprise value? Audience: 
investors and lenders.
Double Materiality (ESRS) Both lenses together: a topic is material if it passes either test. The EU’s 2026 Omnibus kept this principle while cutting datapoints.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 15

S E C T I O N 2 · I S S B
IFRS S1 and S2: The Investor Baseline
Issued in June 2023 by the International Sustainability Standards Board, effective from 1 January 2024 wherever a jurisdiction adopts them.
Four Pillars (from TCFD) IFRS S1 asks for governance, strategy, risk management, and metrics and targets for sustainability-related risks 
and opportunities.
IFRS S2 for Climate Adds Scope 1, 2 and 3 GHG emissions measured under the GHG Protocol, climate resilience and scenario 
analysis, and industry-based metrics.
SASB Standards Industry-specific metrics for 77 industries, now maintained by the ISSB, make disclosures comparable within a 
sector.
Reported With the Financials Sustainability information is reported at the same time and for the same period as the financial statements, 
tying it to financial-reporting discipline.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 16

S E C T I O N 2 · G R I
GRI Standards: The Impact Lens
The most widely used voluntary standards, organised as universal, topic, and sector standards.
Universal Standards (2021) GRI 1 (foundation), GRI 2 (general disclosures), and GRI 3 (material topics). In force since 1 January 2023, with 
impact materiality as the organising idea.
Topic Standards GRI 101 Biodiversity (effective 1 January 2026), plus GRI 102 Climate Change and GRI 103 Energy, published June 
2025 and effective 1 January 2027, replacing GRI 305 and GRI 302.
What GRI 102 Adds Emissions across Scopes 1–3, targets, transition plans, and impacts on workers and communities (just 
transition).
Working Together In June 2025 GRI and the IFRS Foundation said organisations can use GRI 102 with IFRS S2 to report on both 
impacts and financial risks and opportunities.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 17

S E C T I O N 2 · C O N V E R G E N C E
How Far Along Is the World?
28
Jurisdictions that had adopted ISSB 
Standards on a voluntary or 
mandatory basis by April 2026, with 
12 more planning to (S&P Global 
tracking)
36–39
Jurisdictions the IFRS Foundation 
counted in 2025 as using, or taking 
steps toward, ISSB Standards
≈ 40%
Estimated alignment of India’s BRSR 
with IFRS S2, per an ORF analysis; 
BRSR was built around TCFD and GRI
≈ 60%
Cut in mandatory ESRS datapoints 
under the EU’s revised standards 
adopted in July 2026
Convergence is real but uneven: jurisdictions adopt, adapt, or simplify. Expect “collect once, report many” to remain the practical rule for years.
Sources: S&P Global ISSB tracker (April 2026); IFRS Foundation jurisdictional counts (2025); ORF (BRSR interoperability); EU revised ESRS (July 2026).
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 18

◆ INTERACTIVE C A S E S T U D Y
Simplification vs. Comparability: The EU’s 2025–26 Reset
Omnibus I Directive (EU) 2026/470 and the revised ESRS
After the first wave of CSRD reporting, the EU cut the scope of mandatory reporting and rewrote its standards. The Directive was adopted on 24 February 2026 and 
entered into force on 18 March 2026.
Who Reports Now
Only companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than €450 million net turnover 
(previously about 250 employees or €50 million). The Commission estimated roughly 80% 
fewer companies in scope.
The Standards
The revised ESRS, adopted on 3 July 2026, cut mandatory datapoints by roughly 60%, drop 
sector-specific standards, and apply from financial year 2027.
What Survived
Double materiality remains the foundation: in-scope companies must still assess both 
impact and financial materiality.
The Trade-off
Supporters point to lower burden. Critics worry that fewer reporters and fewer datapoints 
reduce comparability and coverage. Both effects are real; weigh them.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 19

S E C T I O N 2 · I N D I A
BRSR, BRSR Core and Assurance in India
SEBI’s framework is mandatory, phased, and increasingly assured.
BRSR Mandatory since FY 2022–23 for the top 1,000 listed companies by market capitalisation, filed with the annual 
report and structured around the nine principles of the National Guidelines on Responsible Business Conduct.
BRSR Core
A focused set of KPIs under nine attributes. Assessment or assurance phases in from the top 150 (FY 2023–24) 
to the top 1,000 (FY 2026–27); in December 2024 SEBI allowed a choice between “assessment” and 
“assurance”.
Assurance Standard ICAI’s Standard on Sustainability Assurance (SSA 5000), modelled on the global ISSA 5000, was issued in 2026 
with a reported effective date of 1 April 2027.
Open Gaps An ORF analysis estimates BRSR is about 40% aligned with IFRS S2 and notes that covering only the top 1,000 
firms captures less than half of India’s emissions footprint.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 20

◆ INTERACTIVE M A T C H T H E Q U E S T I O N T O T H E F R A M E W O R K
Which Framework Answers This?
For each question, choose the framework that is built to answer it.
1 How does our company affect communities and ecosystems, regardless of financial effect?
2 Which climate risks could change our enterprise value, and how are they governed?
3 How do we count Scope 1, 2 and 3 emissions consistently?
4 Is our 2030 emissions target consistent with a 1.5°C pathway?
5 Which industry-specific metrics should a steel company disclose to investors?
6 How do we report the impacts of our energy use (GRI 103)?
GRI ISSB GHG PROT. SBTi

From Data to Disclosure
Reporting is a data process before it is a document. The controls decide whether it can be trusted.

S E C T I O N 3 · T H E R E P O R T I N G C Y C L E
Six Steps From Boundary to Published Disclosure
The cycle repeats every year, and each step leaves evidence the next one relies on.
1. Scope & Boundary Decide the reporting entity, period, and which operations and value-chain parts are in.
2. Materiality Identify which topics matter (impact, financial, or both) and document the method.
3. Collect & Calculate Gather activity data and apply emission factors and conversion rules consistently.
4. Control & Review Reconcile to invoices and meters, test for anomalies, and keep an audit trail.
5. Assure Independent limited or reasonable assurance on selected disclosures.
6. Disclose & Tag Publish in the required framework and format, with machine-readable tagging where required.

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
A Materiality Screen Under Three Lenses
G I V E N
Four topics scored 1–5 for (impact, financial): GHG emissions (5, 4); water use (4, 
2)
Employee safety (3, 3); data privacy (2, 4)
Threshold: a topic is material on a lens if its score is 3.5 or higher
F O R M U L A
Impact lens: Impact ≥ 3.5 · Financial lens: Financial ≥ 3.5
Double materiality: either test passes
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Impact lens (GRI-style): GHG emissions (5) and water use (4) are material
2 Financial lens (ISSB-style): GHG emissions (4) and data privacy (4) are material
3 Double materiality = union: GHG emissions, water use, and data privacy (3 of 4 topics)
4 Employee safety (3, 3) passes neither lens at this threshold
3 of 4 Topics The lens changes the list: water is material only to impact; data privacy only to finance. Documenting the thresholds and scoring 
method is what makes the screen auditable. (Scores are illustrative.)

S E C T I O N 3 · B O U N D A R I E S
Setting and Holding the Boundary
Numbers are only comparable if the boundary they describe stays stable and disclosed.
Organisational Boundary Equity share, financial control, or operational control (from our footprint lecture). Pick one, apply it consistently, 
and disclose it.
Operational Boundary Which scopes and Scope 3 categories are in. Excluded categories should be named, with reasons.
Alignment With Financial Reporting ISSB asks for sustainability information for the same reporting entity and period as the financial statements, so 
boundaries must reconcile.
Consistency Over Time Changes in boundary or method break comparability, which is why base-year recalculation rules exist.
MEASURING & REPORTING SUSTAINABILITY PERFORMANCE 26

S E C T I O N 3 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Base-Year Recalculation After an Acquisition
G I V E N
Base year 2020 emissions: 100,000 tCO₂e; company policy: recalculate if a 
structural change exceeds 5%
In 2024 the company acquires a plant that emitted 12,000 tCO₂e in 2020
2024 emissions, including the new plant: 104,000 tCO₂e
F O R M U L A
Significance = Structural change ÷ Base-year emissions
Recalculated Base = Original Base + Acquired Emissions
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Significance: 12,000 ÷ 100,000 = 12%, above the 5% threshold, so recalculate
2 Recalculated base year: 100,000 + 12,000 = 112,000 tCO₂e
3 Against the unadjusted base: 104,000 vs 100,000 looks like +4%
4 Against the recalculated base: 104,000 vs 112,000 is −7.1%, the like-for-like change
−7.1%, Not +4% Without recalculation, the acquisition makes a real reduction look like an increase. The rule keeps the comparison like for like. 
(Figures are illustrative.)

S E C T I O N 3 · D A T A Q U A L I T Y
What Makes Sustainability Data Auditable
Assurance practitioners test the process as much as the number.
Primary Before Secondary Use metered or invoiced data where possible; estimate with emission factors only where measurement is 
impractical, and label estimates as such.
Versioned Methods Record the emission-factor source and year (for example the CEA grid factor) so any number can be reproduced 
later.
Reconciliation Tie totals to invoices, meters, or the general ledger, and investigate unexplained variances before publishing.
Restatement Discipline When an error or method change is found, restate prior years and disclose why, rather than quietly changing the 
series.

Credibility & Assurance
A disclosure is only as valuable as a reader’s reason to believe it.

S E C T I O N 4 · L E V E L S O F A S S U R A N C E
Limited vs. Reasonable Assurance
Limited Assurance Reasonable Assurance
The practitioner mainly makes inquiries and applies analytical procedures; the 
conclusion is stated negatively (“nothing has come to our attention…”).
The practitioner gathers extensive evidence, tests controls, and samples data; 
the conclusion is stated positively (“in our opinion, fairly stated”).
A lower level of assurance: quicker and less costly. A higher level of assurance, closer to a financial audit: slower and costlier.
A common starting point when a new reporting regime begins. The higher bar. India’s BRSR Core was framed around it, though SEBI later 
allowed an “assessment” option.
Risk: readers over-read “assured” as “audited”. Risk: the scope may cover only selected disclosures, not the whole report.

S E C T I O N 4 · S T A N D A R D S
ISSA 5000 and India’s SSA 5000
Assurance is getting its own global standard.
ISSA 5000 Published by the IAASB in November 2024: the first comprehensive global standard for sustainability assurance, 
covering limited and reasonable assurance on any sustainability topic or framework.
Effective Date For periods beginning on or after 15 December 2026, wherever a jurisdiction adopts it. It replaces ISAE 3410 for 
greenhouse-gas assurance when it takes effect.
India ICAI’s SSA 5000, based on the international standard, is reported to take effect from 1 April 2027 for the top 
1,000 listed companies, and for voluntary use by others.
What It Means for Reporters Strengthen internal controls over ESG data now: weak controls turn into modified assurance conclusions.

S E C T I O N 4 · R E D F L A G S
Four Warning Signs in a Sustainability Report
Use these as a reader, and as a preparer checking your own draft.
Moving Goalposts The base year, boundary, or method changes without disclosure or restatement, so the trend cannot be 
checked.
Intensity-Only Storytelling Intensity improves while absolute totals are omitted or rising (our worked example).
Selective Coverage Scope 3 or the largest impacts are missing, while minor ones are reported in detail.
Assurance Ambiguity A report says “verified” without saying who, to what level, and which disclosures were covered.

S E C T I O N 4 · W O R K E D E X A M P L E
Why the Scope 2 Revision Matters: Annual vs. Hourly Matching
G I V E N
A data centre uses 10,000 MWh a year and buys solar certificates equal to 10,000 
MWh
Solar output covers only 60% of consumption in the hours it is actually used 
(illustrative)
Grid emission factor for unmatched hours: 0.7 tCO₂e per MWh (illustrative)
F O R M U L A
Market-based Emissions = Unmatched Consumption × Grid Factor
S T E P - BY - S T E P C A L C U L A T I O N
1 Annual matching (today): certificates cover 100% of annual use, so market-based Scope 2 = 0 tCO₂e
2 Hourly matching (proposed): unmatched share = 1 − 0.60 = 40%
3 Unmatched consumption: 10,000 × 0.40 = 4,000 MWh
4 Emissions: 4,000 × 0.7 = 2,800 tCO₂e
0 → 2,800 tCO₂e
The GHG Protocol’s 2025 consultation proposed hourly matching and deliverability for market-based claims. Still under revision: a 
final standard is expected in 2027, with implementation likely from 2028.

A Reporting Readiness Checklist
Before the first number is published, you should be able to answer yes to each of these.
Metrics Defined Every metric has a unit, formula, owner, and source, and passes the five tests.
Materiality Documented The method, thresholds, and results are written down and approved.
Boundary & Base Year Set Entity, scopes, base year and recalculation policy are disclosed and consistent.
Controls in Place Reconciliations, lineage, versioned factors, and review are operating and evidenced.
Assurance-Ready The level and scope of assurance are agreed, and the evidence file is organised.
Framework Mapping Done Each disclosure maps to the frameworks the company must or chooses to follow.
